title: Where the Stoics stop
hookLine: Stoicism doesn't settle every question about God, grace or meaning, and other paths say much more

lines: A MAP HONEST ABOUT ITS EDGES.
cards: A good map is honest about its edges. Old maps sometimes left blank space where the mapmakers hadn't been, and that blank was a kind of truthfulness: we don't know what's here.
After almost a full year on the porch, with Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus, it would be easy to treat Stoicism as a map of everything. It isn't.
The Stoics themselves left blank spaces, or disagreed among themselves, on some of the biggest questions people ask. Before summing up the year, here's the edge of the map.

teach.h: GOD AS REASON, NOT A PERSON.
teach.b: First, God. The Stoics spoke of God often: Zeus, nature, reason, the logos running through all things, as in Cleanthes' hymn. In the Stoic texts, God is usually the reason and fire within the universe itself.

Epictetus can speak warmly of God as a father, but the texts tell no story of God making promises to a people or entering history. Whether the cosmos can love you back is a question they mostly leave aside. Second, death.
The Stoics didn't agree. Cleanthes held that all souls last until the world's great burning; Chrysippus said only the souls of the wise.
Marcus keeps returning to the options without choosing: scattering, change, or something else. Whichever it is, his advice is the same: live well now. Third, grace.
In Stoicism, virtue is the one thing entirely up to you. That's its strength.
But it leaves little room for help or forgiveness given freely from beyond yourself, unearned. Religious traditions speak about exactly that, each in its own way. Fourth, meaning in suffering.
Seneca wrote a whole essay asking why good people suffer, and his answers, training, testing, nature's order, satisfy some readers and not others.
Other paths, religious and philosophical, offer their own long answers, with their own scriptures, teachers and communities. The porch was never meant to be a whole house.
It's a good place to stand, look out, and notice that the questions go on past the railing. And so ends a week of hard days and good ones.

how: Some readers of the Stoics use the philosophy for daily practice while looking to religious traditions, other philosophies or their own reflection for questions about God, death and grace.

games.q: after a year on the porch, you find a big question the Stoics don't answer. what does the porch suggest?
o: name the question honestly and keep it open
games.why: a good map is honest about its edges; the questions go on past the railing.

practice: Sit quietly and ask: of all the big questions, which one does Stoicism leave open for me, about God, or death, or forgiveness, or why things happen?
Don't rush to answer; just find the question and say it to yourself in your own words. Notice how it feels to hold a question without an answer.
